General Introduction
Over the past decade, personal ﬁtness and athletic conditioning have become increasingly
integrated with digital technologies. Fitness enthusiasts and athletes seek accessible mobile
applications to organize their training routines, monitor personal progress, and maintain
consistent motivation. Concurrently, certiﬁed ﬁtness coaches and personal trainers require
specialized software tools to supervise clients, structure individualized training programs, and
coordinate consultations without relying on fragmented spreadsheets and informal messaging
channels.
The GoFit project emerges directly from this operational context. Developed within
Antigone Creative Agency in fulﬁllment of the graduation requirements for the National
Engineering Diploma in Computer Science at ESPRIT, GoFit is designed as an integrated
ﬁtness and athletic coaching ecosystem. The platform bridges the divide between independent
training and guided professional coaching by uniting athletes, certiﬁed trainers, and platform
administrators within a coherent, secure digital environment.
The primary objective of the project is to deliver a streamlined software solution that uniﬁes
workout creation, active session tracking, anthropometric evolution monitoring, and personal
coach interaction, while providing back-oﬃce administrators with centralized tools for catalog
curation, coach-proﬁle review, and platform governance.
To provide a comprehensive academic and technical account of the design and realization
of GoFit, this report is structured into six chapters:
• Chapter 1 (Project Study) outlines the industrial and organizational context
at Antigone Creative Agency, states the problem deﬁnition, analyzes the
fragmented-workﬂow scenario and its evidence limits, introduces the conceptual
architecture of GoFit, and details the adopted Scrum development methodology and
UML modeling standards.
• Chapter 2 (Sprint 0) deﬁnes the system actors, functional requirements, non-functional
quality attributes, AI and privacy boundaries, the Product Backlog, sprint scheduling,
and the global use case perimeter.
• Chapter 3 (Sprint 1) details the design and implementation of foundational
capabilities, including user authentication, onboarding personalization, the categorized
exercise library, custom workout template builder, active session tracker with rest timing,
and conditional retry of existing-session completion updates.
• Chapter 4 (Sprint 2) focuses on advanced athletic progression tracking, covering
longitudinal bodyweight and performance metrics, daily macronutrient logging, and
privacy-preserving computer vision workﬂows for anthropometric evolution.
• Chapter 5 (Sprint 3) presents the personal coaching marketplace, session pack

• Chapter 6 (Deployment and Closing Phase) documents the hardware and software

3 Problem Statement
Many ﬁtness users rely on several disconnected tools: one application for workout planning,
another for nutrition, a spreadsheet for body measurements, messaging applications for
coach communication, and separate calendars or payment tools for coaching sessions. This
fragmentation reduces engagement, creates duplicated data entry, and makes long-term
progress harder to understand.
For coaches, the issue is also operational. Managing client proﬁles, programs,
bookings, messages, session packs, and progress follow-up across separate services increases
administrative workload and reduces the quality of personalized support. Administrators
also need a centralized interface to manage users, coaches, exercises, workouts, analytics, and
platform content.
A second diﬃculty concerns personalization. Fitness applications often ask users to follow
predeﬁned programs without considering recent activity, readiness, goals, progress, or coach
context. Coaches may personalize plans manually, but this becomes time-consuming as the
number of clients grows. GoFit therefore investigates AI-assisted recommendations and
AI-generated coach brieﬁngs to support decision-making while keeping the coach and user in
control.
A third diﬃculty concerns body-progress tracking. Users often want visual and numerical
feedback about body evolution, but manual tape measurements are irregular and progress
photos are hard to interpret objectively. Computer vision can help extract pose and silhouette
indicators, but it also introduces technical constraints: photo quality, camera angle, clothing,
segmentation quality, privacy, model performance, and the fact that consumer photos cannot
produce perfect circumference measurements without validation.
4 Study of Existing Conditions
The existing-condition analysis considers a fragmented workﬂow in which training, nutrition,
measurements, coaching communication and appointments are maintained in separate tools. It
is a project problem scenario used to derive requirements, rather than a comparative market
survey or an observation of every ﬁtness application. The retained project material does not
establish a representative user sample, measured administrative workload or adoption statistics.
Consequently, the following analysis identiﬁes integration needs without ranking competing
products or claiming that they universally lack these capabilities.
For the client, a workout log, food diary and measurement history maintained separately
make it necessary to consult several records when reviewing progress. The requirement is
to associate those records with the same account while preserving their distinct meanings:
prescribed repetitions diﬀer from recorded completion, and estimated body dimensions diﬀer
from independently measured reference values.
For the coach, separate messages, calendars, payment records and program documents can
make it diﬃcult to connect an appointment with its client context. The proposed integration
therefore concerns the continuity between discovery, booking, communication, programs and
follow-up. No reduction in administrative time or improvement in coaching outcomes has been
measured in this project.
14

For progress tracking, manually entered measurements and photographs provide diﬀerent
kinds of information. Their interpretation depends on capture conditions, measurement
procedure and consistency over time. This motivates recording provenance and allowing
correction of an estimated draft; it does not establish that computer vision is more accurate
than a standardized manual measurement protocol.
For administration, the project requires identiﬁable access boundaries, catalog management,
coach-proﬁle review and inspection of operational records. Centralizing these functions can
support oversight, but does not itself prove policy correctness, complete audit coverage or
independent professional accreditation. For intelligent assistance, the identiﬁed need is to
prepare contextual drafts and reminders; response quality, scheduled execution and human
review must be evaluated separately.
5 Limits and Inconveniences of the Existing Workﬂow
The problem scenario leads to ﬁve design concerns. These are requirements to address and
assess, rather than measured deﬁciencies shared by all existing products:
• Fragmented records: Separate training, nutrition and coaching records make
cross-domain review less direct and can require repeated entry of the same context.
• Coordination overhead: Independent program documents, appointments and
messages require explicit reconciliation; the project does not quantify the time involved.
• Uncertain progress interpretation: Changes in capture or measurement conditions
can aﬀect comparability. Neither manual entry nor an AI estimate alone establishes
body-composition accuracy.
• Operational traceability: Role-based interfaces and selected audit records must be
assessed against the actions they actually protect and record.
• Privacy and access boundaries: Local captures, remotely stored records and
external-service requests need distinct access and retention rules. Combining them in
one application does not automatically resolve those risks.

1.2 Functional Requirements
Functional requirements deﬁne the core capabilities, operations, and services that the GoFit
ecosystem must deliver to satisfy stakeholder needs. To ensure rigorous academic traceability
without duplicating the product backlog, these requirements are organized into eight distinct
functional domains:
• FR-01: Authentication, Onboarding, and Proﬁle Management (Actors: User,
Coach, Administrator | Priority: High): The platform must support secure
email/password registration, login, password recovery, and hardware-persisted JWT
session management via Supabase GoTrue. It must enforce a structured multi-step
onboarding questionnaire capturing athlete goals, ﬁtness levels, equipment availability,
and dietary preferences, with automatic role-based navigation routing.
• FR-02: Exercise Catalog and Custom Workout Planning (Actor: User |
Priority: High): The application must provide a searchable, faceted exercise library
categorized by target muscle groups, diﬃculty tiers, and required equipment. Users
must be able to construct customized workout routines, reorder exercise sequences, and
conﬁgure target set, repetition, and load parameters.
• FR-03: Active Workout Session Execution and Rest Timing (Actor: User |
Priority: High): The mobile client must provide an interactive active-session interface
tracking completed sets, reps, load, and RPE ratings. It must incorporate an animated
circular rest timer with conﬁgurable intervals, audio chimes, tactile haptic feedback, and
resilient local oﬄine queue persistence in case of gym network loss.
• FR-04: Anthropometric Progress and AI-Assisted Body Measurement
(Actor: User | Priority: High): Users must be able to log bodyweight, track strength
progression curves, and maintain visual progress photo galleries. The system must
support an on-device computer vision workﬂow using MediaPipe Pose Landmarker and
Selﬁe Segmentation to extract silhouette features from front and side photos, generating
editable draft measurements that require explicit user veriﬁcation.
• FR-05: Nutrition Logging and Dietary Preference Filtering (Actor: User
| Priority: Medium): The platform must provide daily macronutrient and caloric
tracking with animated visual budgets, barcode scanning via OpenFoodFacts integration,
reusable saved meal templates, and allergen/dislike exclusion ﬁlters.
• FR-06: Coach Discovery, Session Booking, and Messaging (Actors: User,
Coach | Priority: Medium): Athletes must be able to browse veriﬁed coach proﬁles,
inspect specialties and client reviews, purchase multi-session packages via Stripe
PaymentSheet, reserve calendar slots, and engage in real-time encrypted messaging.
• FR-07: Coach Workspace, Client Rosters, and Program Assignment (Actor:
Coach | Priority: Medium): Coaches must have access to a dedicated mobile
workspace to review client performance, inspect check-in submissions and progress
photos, assign tailored workout and nutrition plans, and receive AI-synthesized

post-session brieﬁngs.
• FR-08: Web Administration, Content Moderation, and Analytics (Actor:
Administrator | Priority: High): Administrators must have access to a protected

1.3 Non-Functional Requirements
Non-functional requirements specify the architectural qualities, operational constraints,
and quality attributes that the platform must satisfy to ensure security, performance,
maintainability, and usability:
• NFR-01: Security and Access Governance: Protected operations should
authenticate callers and enforce record-level authorization. Exposed application tables
should use appropriate RLS policies, and privileged credentials should remain in trusted
server-side, administration or automation contexts. Enabled RLS and JWT validation
are controls to verify, not proof that every policy or handler is correct.
• NFR-02: Performance and Real-Time Responsiveness: The intended targets are
smooth mobile rendering, interaction latency below 100 milliseconds and administrative
page loading below 1.5 seconds under a deﬁned workload. The earlier 60 FPS objective
is a design target. No retained proﬁling or load-test run establishes these values,
background-timer reliability or large-dataset responsiveness.
• NFR-03: Maintainability, Modularity, and Code Quality: Presentation, state,
domain services and migrations should remain separated, with shared TypeScript
interfaces supporting consistency. Full type safety is an objective rather than an achieved
guarantee: the latest mobile project-wide check retains the 12 diagnostics reported in
the QA section.
• NFR-04: Usability, Ergonomics, and Accessibility: Interfaces should provide
readable contrast, text scaling, English/French localization, feedback and clear empty
states. The retained settings contrast checks cover selected styles and modeled surfaces;
native visual acceptance and whole-application accessibility are not established.

• NFR-05: Scalability and Extensibility: Modular services, appropriate relational
constraints and indexing should support future growth and integrations. Horizontal
scalability, deployment capacity and interoperability require explicit workload and
integration tests; schema structure alone does not demonstrate them.
1.4 AI and Privacy Constraints
Because GoFit handles personal biometric data, progress photos, and automated
recommendations, the integration of artiﬁcial intelligence is governed by strict ethical,
architectural, and privacy constraints:
• Human-in-the-Loop Review: Measurement drafts are presented for correction before
the user saves them, and recommended workouts have a user-save interaction. Coach
brieﬁngs diﬀer: the backend can cache generated text when requested, before a separate
review action. Advisory presentation therefore does not mean that every generated output
requires human conﬁrmation before any database write.
• Non-Medical Boundary: GoFit positions all AI features strictly as wellness, ﬁtness,
and training aids. The application explicitly disclaims medical diagnostics, clinical body
composition evaluations, and medical rehabilitation guidance.
• Context-Scoped Prompts: Backend templates constrain the requested output and
recommendation code checks exercise identiﬁers. The brieﬁng request includes selected
proﬁle data, workout history and private coach notes sent to Groq; anonymization is
not established. Instructions and output checks mitigate some risks but do not prove
prevention of prompt injection, hallucinations or unsafe advice.
• Privileged Credential Isolation: Privileged database and provider secrets should
remain in trusted backend, administration and n8n environments. The inspected
payment/video code reads provider secrets server-side; public client conﬁguration is a
separate category. This source review is not a complete audit of compiled binaries, logs,
deployment settings or repository history.
• On-Device Computer Vision Processing: The inspected pose/segmentation ﬂow
reads local captures and stores reviewed numerical results rather than uploading captures
for that inference path. Progress-photo uploads and external language-model requests are
separate ﬂows. Local inference does not establish complete privacy, storage-security or
cross-platform guarantees.
Following the comprehensive identiﬁcation of system actors, functional requirements, and
non-functional constraints, the project requires a structured development methodology to
organize implementation into manageable, iterative delivery cycles. The subsequent section
formalizes the application of Scrum within GoFit, deﬁning the team roles, product backlog
decomposition, and sprint distribution.

3.3 Workout Core and Rest Timer
The workout core was implemented around the distinction between a workout template and
an executed workout session. A workout template deﬁnes the exercises, order, diﬃculty, target
muscle groups, and expected conﬁguration. A workout session stores timestamps, duration,
notes and exercise snapshots with conﬁgured sets/repetitions, entered weights and completion
ﬂags. Those snapshots do not independently measure performed repetitions or RPE. This
separation is essential because the same workout can be performed many times while producing
diﬀerent session histories.
The rest timer was treated as a real workout tool rather than a decorative countdown. It
includes start, pause, resume, warning cues, haptic feedback, audio cues, auto-advance options,
and persisted preferences. This improves usability during training because users often interact
with the timer under fatigue and need clear feedback without navigating away from the session.

3.4 Oﬄine Workout Resiliency and Fault-Tolerant Queue
A critical architectural challenge encountered during gym testing is network instability. Physical
gym environments frequently feature thick reinforced concrete walls or subterranean weight
rooms where cellular connectivity drops completely. Without proper handling, ﬁnishing a
session in an oﬄine state results in lost workout telemetry, user frustration, and broken streaks.
To ensure bulletproof reliability, GoFit introduces an optimistic oﬄine workout queue service
(GoFitMobile/src/services/offlineQueue.ts). When the user completes a session and the API
request fails due to network unreachability, the application intercepts the error, persists the
session payload securely
into local AsyncStorage, and presents immediate positive feedback so the user’s ﬂow is
uninterrupted. Concurrently, a NetInfo network listener registered at the application root
(App.tsx) detects when Internet connectivity is re-established. The queue processor then
automatically dequeues, synchronizes, and conﬁrms the stored workout sessions against
Supabase in the background with deduplication safeguards.
3.5 Cloudﬂare R2 Video Demonstration Streaming Pipeline
High-deﬁnition visual instruction is crucial for proper exercise execution and injury prevention.
However, storing hundreds of high-resolution MP4 video demonstrations directly in standard
database byte storage or high-egress cloud buckets introduces severe egress bandwidth costs
47

and latency bottlenecks.
GoFit solves this through a dedicated Cloudﬂare R2 object storage architecture utilizing
the S3-compatible A WS SDK (@aws-sdk/client-s3). A catalog of over 90 unique exercise videos
(encompassing 99 canonical exercises in Supabase) was uploaded to an R2 bucket (goﬁt-content)
with zero egress bandwidth charges. On the mobile client, ExerciseDetailScreen leverages
expo-video with hardware-accelerated playback, automatic loop buﬀering, and smooth scrub
controls, ensuring ﬂuid video streaming with minimal device battery drain.

3.2 Data Interpretation and User Feedback
A key design point in Sprint 2 is that GoFit should not only store values; it should help the
user interpret them. For example, workout history becomes useful when the app can show
consistency, completed sessions, training load, and trends. Body measurements become useful
when the user can compare corrected values over time and understand why an AI draft may
be uncertain. Nutrition entries become useful when they are reusable and connected to habits
rather than isolated forms.
3.3 Client Nutrition Preferences & Intelligent Dietary Exclusion Engine
Nutrition is deeply personalized: ﬁtness clients have speciﬁc dietary philosophies (e.g., vegan,
keto, Mediterranean), critical food allergies (e.g., peanuts, lactose, gluten), and strong personal
food dislikes. Standard ﬁtness trackers often force users to manually ﬁlter foods or ignore their
preferences completely.
In GoFit, the nutrition module was expanded with a robust preference architecture. The
user_proﬁles database table was extended with dietary_preferences (TEXT[]), food_allergies
(TEXT[]), and food_dislikes (TEXT[]) supported by PostgreSQL GIN indexes. During
onboarding (OnboardingScreenNutrition.tsx), new users explicitly deﬁne their allergies
and disliked ingredients. On the NutritionScreen, an interactive callout alerts users with
incomplete dietary proﬁles, routing them directly to complete their conﬁguration.
Crucially, this data is enforced in food search and recommendation workﬂows. When
searching for foods in AddFoodScreen.tsx, nutritionService.searchFoods() dynamically injects
67

SQL negation ﬁlters
(.not(’name’, ’ilike’, ’%’ + exclusion + ’%’)) to strictly exclude all disliked foods and
allergens from the search results, ensuring clients are never presented with meals they dislike
or cannot safely consume.
3.4 Hydration Tracking and Multi-Period Macronutrient Analytics
In addition to qualitative food ﬁltering, GoFit provides comprehensive quantitative nutrition
analytics. The mobile screen integrates an interactive MacroRings visualization that tracks
daily calories, protein, carbohydrates, and healthy fats against personalized caloric targets. A
quick-tap water intake tracker (+250ml / +500ml) encourages daily hydration. To help users
focus on sustainable long-term consistency rather than single-day ﬂuctuations, a 7-day rolling
trend widget calculates average caloric intake and adherence scores across protein, water, and
ﬁber.
The sprint therefore uses feedback patterns such as charts, summaries, empty states,
warnings, and review screens. This is especially important for AI-assisted measurements.
Instead of hiding uncertainty, the application should show quality issues such as poor pose,
incomplete body visibility, weak segmentation, bad framing, or inconsistent scale between
front and side photos.
3.5 AI Body Measurement and Computer Vision Pipeline
One of the most distinctive parts of GoFit is the AI-assisted body measurement feature. Its
objective is to help users follow physical progress from photos, without replacing manual
tape measurements and without claiming medical or tailoring-grade precision. The feature
is designed as an assisted workﬂow: the system analyzes front and side photos, generates draft
values for chest, waist, hip, and shoulder, explains capture-quality issues, then lets the user
review and correct the values before saving them as progress data.
The pipeline starts on the mobile device. The user captures or selects front and side images.
The application runs pose detection to locate key body landmarks, segmentation to isolate the
person
silhouette when available, feature extraction to transform image geometry into measurable
indicators, and a measurement estimator to produce draft values. The result is presented with
conﬁdence, warnings, and manual editing ﬁelds. This design is important because computer
vision can support progress tracking, but a single two-dimensional image cannot directly recover
exact body circumferences in all conditions.

3.7 Pose Detection: MoveNet and MediaPipe
Pose detection is responsible for ﬁnding anatomical landmarks that anchor the measurement
process. In the ﬁrst GoFit prototype, MoveNet Lightning detects 17 keypoints such as nose,
shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. These points are enough to estimate body
orientation and basic proportions, but they are not enough to measure chest, waist, and hip
circumference directly. For example, a shoulder keypoint tells where the shoulder is, but it does
not describe the width of the torso at chest level or the depth of the body from the side view.
The MediaPipe Pose Landmarker Full model improves this stage by producing 33
landmarks and richer metadata. The local module returns image dimensions, pose count,
normalized landmarks, world landmarks when available, and inference time. The GoFit
Android implementation loads the bundled pose_landmarker_full.task asset, decodes the
image URI, applies EXIF rotation, runs MediaPipe detection, and returns a typed result
to the TypeScript layer. This makes the measurement workﬂow more reliable because the
application can inspect landmark visibility, check whether core points are present, and reject
only captures that are genuinely unusable.
The project keeps MoveNet as a fallback because it is already integrated in the mobile
JavaScript service and can continue to support devices or builds where the native MediaPipe
module is not available. This fallback strategy reduces deployment risk while the native module
reaches parity across Android and iOS.
3.8 Segmentation and Body Mask Extraction
Segmentation is the second computer-vision component. Its role is to separate the person from
the background and provide body-outline information. This is necessary because circumference
estimation cannot be based only on joint coordinates. The pose model can locate shoulder,
hip, and torso reference lines; the segmentation mask can then estimate front-view widths and
side-view depths around the chest, waist, and hip levels.
70

The project ﬁrst examined selfie_multiclass_256x256.tflite. That model exposes a 256 x
256 x 6 output rather than a simple binary body mask, which required class selection, argmax
maps, connected-component cleanup, and debugging overlays. Real tests showed that the
resulting mask could be unstable, especially with mirror photos, phone occlusion, and direct
capture conditions. For this reason, the report classiﬁes it as an experimental research artifact
instead of a ﬁnal production model.
The later implementation uses MediaPipe Image Segmenter with selfie_segmenter.tflite
in the local native module. The Android bridge returns conﬁdence masks, category masks,
labels, quality scores, and inference timing. The TypeScript segmentation service decodes
the masks, thresholds the person class, builds a cleaned binary mask, extracts sampled class
grids for debugging, anchors scan lines using pose landmarks, and measures chest, waist, and
hip widths/depths. This gives GoFit a more explainable measurement pipeline because each
generated number can be traced back to pose landmarks, mask rows, and quality gates.

The measurement service builds a structured feature vector before calculating the ﬁnal draft
values. This is a strong architectural choice because the application does not mix raw pixels,
pose conﬁdence, segmentation quality, and ﬁnal centimeter values in a single opaque formula.
Instead, it records the intermediate indicators that explain why a measurement was accepted,
warned, or rejected.

3.7 In-App AI Workout Recommendation and Personalization
The in-app AI workout recommendation feature deserves separate treatment because it is a
user-facing personalization feature, not a computer-vision feature and not an n8n scheduled
automation. Its goal is to generate one practical custom workout from the user’s real GoFit
109

context, then let the user decide whether to save it into the workout library. In the mobile
application, this feature appears as the Adaptive workout card implemented in GoFitMobile/s
rc/components/home/RecommendedWorkouts.tsx.
The mobile ﬂow starts from the home screen. When the user taps the Adaptive workout
card, the component calls workoutRecommendationService.generateAIWorkout from GoFit
Mobile/src/services/workoutRecommendations.ts. This service invokes the Supabase Edge
Function named ai-workout-recommendation. If the response is valid, the card displays the
generated workout name, focus/reason text, number of exercises, and an adaptation label such
as readiness level, days since last workout, coach companion context, and volume adjustment.
If the user accepts the suggestion, the feature saves it as a custom workout with workoutSe
rvice.createCustomWorkout, reloads the workout store, triggers success haptic feedback, and
navigates to the workout detail screen.
On the backend, the ai-workout-recommendation Edge Function authenticates the caller
through the Authorization header before collecting context. It reads the user’s proﬁle, recent
completed workout sessions, the latest daily readiness snapshot, recent health data, the
latest assigned program, any active purchased coach pack, and the exercise catalog. The
function computes an adaptive context before calling the language model. This context
includes readiness level, readiness score, days since last workout, volume adjustment, intensity
guidance, recovery signals, coach-program state, and explicit constraints.
The AI model used for this feature is Groq’s OpenAI-compatible chat completion endpoint
with the model llama-3.3-70b-versatile. The function requests JSON output with a low
temperature and instructs the model to create one workout only, use only exercises from the
provided catalog, avoid invented exercise identiﬁers, reduce volume when readiness is low,
propose moderate catch-up work after several inactive days, and treat the result as optional
companion work when a coach program or active pack exists. This prompt design is important
because it grounds the LLM output in GoFit data instead of allowing generic ﬁtness advice.
The feature also contains post-generation validation. The returned JSON is parsed, every
exercise ID is matched against the real exercise catalog, invalid exercises are discarded, and
the ﬁnal recommendation is rejected if fewer than three valid exercises remain. The maximum
exercise count is also adapted: reduced-volume sessions are limited more strictly than normal
sessions. The response sent back to the mobile app includes the ﬁnal workout name, diﬃculty
set to Custom, focus, reason, image, validated exercise list, and adaptation metadata. This
means the mobile app does not blindly trust the LLM response; it receives a cleaned and
structured result.

2.2 Technologies and Selection Rationale
The principal technology choices support the following implementation goals:
• Expo SDK 54 and React Native provide a shared TypeScript application structure and
access to native device modules. Native dependencies require suitable builds, and code sharing
does not establish feature parity across platforms.
• Supabase supplies managed authentication, database APIs, storage, and realtime
capabilities. Database policies support authenticated access control; service-role callers
operate with elevated privileges and require separate server-side checks. This choice reduces
custom infrastructure without guaranteeing isolation under every application or policy error.
• Next.js App Router separates browser interactions from server-rendered pages, protected
route handlers, and privileged backend/media adapters. The implemented request proxy and
route checks support administrative access control.
• On-device pose and segmentation processing avoids a cloud inference request for the
measurement captures in the inspected ﬂow. Estimates still require quality checks and
user review; local processing alone does not establish accuracy, latency, or complete privacy
guarantees. The separate progress-photo feature can upload photos to managed storage.
• Groq is the conﬁgured provider for the inspected AI handlers and AI Session Prep workﬂow.
Provider/model selection is an implementation choice; no response-time or token-throughput
benchmark is established by these source ﬁles.
2.3 Layered Architecture
The implementation separates several responsibilities, with some direct calls across the
suggested layers:
• Presentation: React Native screens, navigation, and reusable components render data and
handle interaction. Screens also contain local state and, in selected paths such as measurement
saving and checkout initiation, direct Supabase calls.
• Shared state: Zustand stores hold cross-screen data and coordinate selected service
operations. Persistence is conﬁgured for speciﬁc stores and preferences; not every state change
is durably cached.
• Services and adapters: TypeScript modules implement domain operations, transformations,
API access, and device integration. Local native inference and device SDKs execute within the
mobile boundary.
118

• Server execution: Next.js pages, proxy checks, API routes, Supabase Edge Functions, and
n8n workﬂow code have distinct execution contexts. Server credentials and token/payment/AI
handlers are not part of a shared browser or mobile state layer.
2.4 Architecture Patterns: Local Persistence, Retry, and Realtime
Oﬄine support is scoped to implemented paths. Timer preferences are persisted locally.
Workout completion for an already-created session can be queued in AsyncStorage when its
remote update fails and connectivity is reported absent. The application’s connectivity listener
later invokes queue synchronization, retrying updates and removing successful entries. Session
creation still requires the remote request, and the queue does not establish durable storage for
every set interaction, execution while the application is terminated, or guaranteed absence of
data loss. Other operations, including the measurement save path, do not use this workout
queue.
Realtime subscriptions are implemented for selected data, including conversation
messages and workout-session changes. Other screens use explicit refreshes or focus-triggered
queries; nutrition logging and booking creation should not be described as universally
subscription-driven. Source subscriptions establish the intended update mechanism, not
instantaneous delivery on every device. The reviewed structure also does not establish a
separate command/query infrastructure warranting a general CQRS implementation claim.

and uses realtime subscriptions for updates. It also copies a message preview into notiﬁcation
payloads. No client-side encryption/decryption or participant key-management step was

Conclusion
This chapter documents GoFit’s implementation and deployment foundations together
with the limits of the available validation evidence. The October 2026 follow-up supports
speciﬁc Android development-build workﬂows, selected administrative operations and access
restrictions, a native sandbox pack purchase, and backend sandbox session-payment and
reservation checks. Automated regression results strengthen conﬁdence in the cases they
exercise, but the incomplete mobile type check and outstanding integration and device checks
prevent a conclusion of universal requirements compliance or production readiness.
GoFit is therefore presented as a substantial implemented prototype with partially veriﬁed
integrations. Oﬄine resilience, body-measurement accuracy, AI response-time performance,
scheduled notiﬁcation delivery, two-party video reliability, iOS support and production
scalability require dedicated evidence before corresponding guarantees can be made. The next
phase should complete these checks, retest the recent mobile corrections and establish release
conﬁguration and payment recovery appropriate to deployment.

General Conclusion
The GoFit graduation internship project produced a substantial software foundation for
a ﬁtness platform combining client and coach mobile applications, a web administration
panel, and a Supabase backend. The repository contains implementations or foundations
for authentication, onboarding, proﬁle management, workouts, exercise discovery, progress
tracking, nutrition, marketplace and booking workﬂows, communication, coaching programs,
notiﬁcations, analytics and administration. The presence of these implementations does not
imply that every workﬂow has been validated end to end.
Beyond the visible interfaces, the project demonstrates several engineering competencies.
The mobile application required shared application architecture, state management, navigation
design, camera and native-module integration, and Android-oriented testing. The backend
required work on database organization, migrations, row-level security, storage, realtime
communication, Edge Functions and privileged-service separation. The administration panel
required protected server-side access, management operations and analytical views. These
contributions establish an engineering foundation; they do not constitute a complete security
audit or proof of equivalent behavior on every target platform.
The AI dimension contributes a study of computer-vision models, native integration,
segmentation, feature extraction, statistical estimation and validation protocols for body
measurements. These technical elements do not establish measurement accuracy without
comparison against independent references. Language-model features use controlled prompts
and backend or n8n integration to support proposed workouts and session brieﬁngs rather than
autonomous coaching decisions. Five n8n workﬂow exports describe AI session preparation,
booking reminders, check-in reminders, coach daily summaries and administrative summaries;
their presence does not establish successful scheduled execution or push delivery.
The project also reﬂects the evolution of modern software development practice. AI tools
such as Codex were used during development and reporting to accelerate repository analysis,
code navigation, documentation synthesis, and report generation. MCP-style connected
tools made the assistant more useful by grounding work in local ﬁles, oﬃcial documentation,
document-generation utilities, Supabase-related context, automation artifacts, and command
outputs. This use was supervised and veriﬁed through local ﬁles, structural checks, diﬀs,
and project-speciﬁc evidence. The report therefore documents both AI as a GoFit product
capability and AI as a controlled development-support tool.
The later October 2026 audit adds scoped physical-device evidence on one Android
development environment and browser/API evidence for administration and sandbox
payments. It includes a veriﬁed native EUR129 pack purchase with 12 saved credits and a
separate EUR60 standalone-session capture veriﬁed through the backend and administration
panel. These are later corrections and checks, not retrospective proof of completion during the
internship. The native standalone-session checkout and three recent mobile corrections still
require Android retesting, and the project-wide mobile type check remains unsuccessful.
132

Before a production release, further work must establish oﬄine reconciliation, independent
measurement accuracy, reachable AI-generation tests, fresh notiﬁcation delivery and two-party
audio/video behavior. Payment recovery, webhook or equivalent reconciliation, refunds and
payouts also require implementation decisions and validation beyond the synchronous sandbox
scenarios. The iOS MediaPipe path, real-device iOS testing, release builds, production
conﬁguration and deployment-scale behavior remain unﬁnished or unveriﬁed. GoFit should
consequently be regarded as a substantial prototype whose veriﬁed capabilities and remaining
limitations are explicitly distinguished.
